name: Origen's Platonized theology
plain_explanation: Origen tried to explain Christian doctrine using ideas borrowed from Platonist philosophy, such as souls existing before birth and the eventual salvation of everyone, including the devil -- views later judged too unorthodox for the Church to accept.
precise_definition: Origen's synthesis, as set out in De Principiis, holding that nothing is wholly incorporeal except the Trinity; that stars are living, rational (and even sinning) beings; that souls pre-exist their bodies (per Plato) and cycle between soul and Nous; and that ultimately all spirits, even the devil, will be reconciled to Christ and become bodiless -- later condemned as heretical on four counts (pre-existence of souls, pre-existence of Christ's human nature, ethereal resurrection bodies, universal salvation).
why_it_mattered: It is, in Russell's account, the first serious attempt at systematic Christian philosophy, and shows Christian theology's early, close, and eventually uneasy relationship with Neoplatonism (Origen was a fellow student of Ammonius Saccas alongside Plotinus).
historical_origin: Developed in Alexandria in the early-to-mid third century.
examples: Origen's claim that the sun can sin
Origen's belief that even devils will ultimately be saved
objections: Later Church condemnation on the four heresies Russell lists
Saint Jerome's later vehement repudiation of Origen's theological views despite earlier admiring his textual scholarship
competing_positions: Later Nicene/Augustinian orthodoxy, which rejected universal salvation and the pre-existence of souls
influence_on_later_thinkers: Origen's twofold apologetic method (reason plus scriptural/prophetic-miraculous proof) became, per Russell, the standard structure of Christian philosophical argument 'until the Renaissance.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Purely theological/philosophical, though its condemnation illustrates the Church's growing doctrinal policing once it had institutional power.
